summary_en.motivation: To achieve additive manufacturing of dissimilar metals, specifically Ti-alloy to stainless steel, for multi-material components.
summary_en.method: A Cu-alloy interlayer was used in selective laser melting to fabricate a graded interface between Ti-alloy and stainless steel.
summary_en.result: Crack-free joints with improved interfacial strength compared to direct joining were obtained.
summary_en.validation: Tensile testing was conducted to validate the mechanical integrity of the interface.

papers.title: Comparison between Mechanical Properties and Structures of a Rolled and a 3D-Printed Stainless Steel
papers.abstract: In this work selective laser melting was successfully utilized to produce 316 stainless steel bulk specimens. Although this technology provides many advantages compared to conventional shaping processes, little residual porosity may be a problem for some applications where high strength is required. The objective of this work was to determine, through data analysis, a mechanical and metallographic comparison between thin sheets made by using different manufacturing technologies: Cold rolling and additive manufacturing. This comparison was useful to understand whether it could be more advantageous to use the prototyping for new mechanical components. The results show that the additive manufactured steel, due to its microstructure, is characterized by a higher yield strength and by a lower elongation and ultimate tensile strength.

summary_en.motivation: This study compares the mechanical properties and microstructures of cold-rolled and selective laser melted 316 stainless steel to assess the advantages of additive manufacturing for mechanical components.
summary_en.method: Bulk specimens were fabricated via selective laser melting and cold rolling, followed by tensile testing and metallographic analysis.
summary_en.result: The additively manufactured steel exhibited higher yield strength but lower elongation and ultimate tensile strength compared to the rolled steel.
summary_en.validation: Experimental validation was conducted through mechanical tensile testing and microstructural characterization.

papers.title: Effect of strut cross section and strut defect on tensile properties of cubic cellular structure
papers.abstract: Selective laser melting (SLM) process is used to produce complex geometries for various applications such as biomedical and aerospace industries. However, one of the limitations with respect to this process is the introduction of geometrical defects during the manufacturing process. The presence of these defects makes it difficult to predict their mechanical behaviour. The present work focuses on the cubic lattice structures and their geometrical deviations from the as-designed structures caused by defects like strut oversizing, varying thickness, and strut waviness. The defects were introduced in finite element modelling by using different cross-sections along a strut and joining them to form smooth solid struts. The modelling of defects was validated by comparing with experimental data. The results indicate an appreciable difference between as-designed and as-built structures. It was observed that varying the strut thickness had a major effect on the strength of the structures. Additionally, an elliptical cross-section better matched the tensile behaviour of the as-built structures rather than a rectangular cross-section.

summary_zh.motivation: 研究SLM制造晶格结构中支柱缺陷对力学行为的影响。
summary_zh.method: 通过有限元建模引入不同截面形状的支柱缺陷，并与实验拉伸数据对比验证。
summary_zh.result: 支柱厚度变化对强度影响最大，椭圆截面比矩形截面更匹配实验行为。
summary_zh.validation: 通过实验拉伸测试验证有限元模型的准确性。

summary_en.motivation: This work investigates how geometric defects in SLM-fabricated cubic lattice structures affect their mechanical behavior.
summary_en.method: Finite element models with varying strut cross-sections and defects were validated against experimental tensile tests.
summary_en.result: Strut thickness variation significantly affects strength, and elliptical cross-sections better reproduce as-built tensile behavior than rectangular ones.
summary_en.validation: Experimental tensile testing of SLM-fabricated cubic lattices was used to validate the finite element predictions.

summary_en.motivation: To engineer a cell-laden hydrogel microfibrous patch for guided tissue regeneration using a bottom-up assembly approach.
summary_en.method: Microfibers were fabricated and assembled into a patch structure via a bottom-up engineering strategy.
summary_en.result: The patch supported cell viability and promoted tissue regeneration in vitro and in vivo.
summary_en.validation: Validation was performed using cell culture experiments and animal models.
